turns.content: Each of 2009 nondegenerate triangles has one blue, one red, and one white side. Sort lengths within each colour as b_1<=...<=b_2009, r_1<=...<=r_2009, and w_1<=...<=w_2009. Prove that at least one same-index triple (b_j,r_j,w_j) forms a nondegenerate triangle.
Check the strictness of that guarantee. If some sorted lengths coincide, does the argument still give a strict triangle inequality rather than a degenerate triangle?

To test whether the guarantee is sharp, consider original triangles with one blue, one red, and one white side: (blue,red,white)=(3i,3i+1/2,1) for i=1,...,2008, and (3*2009,1,3*2009+1/2) for the last triangle. Verify that every original triple is nondegenerate.
How does the colour assignment in the last triangle differ from the first 2008, and how will that affect sorting the red and white lengths separately?
Sort the constructed family by colour and write the blue, red, and white side-length sequences.

Classify the sorted triples (b_j,r_j,w_j) using only the converse Pythagorean equality: count a triple as nondegenerate precisely when its largest squared side equals the sum of the other two squared sides. Apply this test to the first, intermediate, and last indices.
Combine the universal guarantee with this example to determine the largest integer k that is always guaranteed.
